clinicalPearls: Persistently dilated, poorly reactive pupils present from birth with an essentially normal-appearing but functionally unresponsive iris
Both light and near responses are typically impaired, and pupils show little reaction to pharmacological miotics or mydriatics
The condition reflects maldevelopment or dysfunction of the iris sphincter and dilator smooth muscle rather than a neurological lesion
Photophobia and difficulty with near focusing are common because of the fixed large aperture
Reported in association with ACTA2 mutations as part of a smooth-muscle dysfunction syndrome that includes patent ductus arteriosus and cerebral and aortic vascular disease
Structural iris disorders such as aniridia and iris coloboma, and pharmacological or traumatic mydriasis, must be excluded
Management is supportive with tinted or photochromic lenses and refractive correction; the systemic associations may require cardiovascular and cerebrovascular surveillance
reference.pathophysiology: Congenital mydriasis is characterised by fixed pupillary dilatation from birth due to a primary abnormality of the iris musculature. Rather than a defect of the parasympathetic pathway, the sphincter pupillae and dilator smooth muscle are maldeveloped or dysfunctional, so the pupil neither constricts to light and near effort nor responds normally to pharmacological agents. In a recognised subset, mutations in ACTA2, which encodes smooth-muscle alpha-actin, disturb smooth muscle throughout the body, producing not only iris dysfunction but also patent ductus arteriosus, aortic aneurysm and dissection, and cerebrovascular disease. The fixed large pupil impairs the eye's ability to regulate retinal illumination and contributes to photophobia and near difficulty.
additionalDifferentials: Iris coloboma and other structural iris defects
Third nerve palsy with pupil involvement
additionalInvestigations: Slit-lamp examination of iris structure and pupillary margin
Pharmacological pupil testing to assess sphincter and dilator responsiveness
Cycloplegic refraction and assessment of near function
Genetic testing for ACTA2 and related smooth-muscle genes
Echocardiography and vascular imaging where a smooth-muscle syndrome is suspected
redFlags: Features suggesting an ACTA2 smooth-muscle syndrome with aortic aneurysm or dissection risk
Signs of a patent ductus arteriosus or other cardiac anomaly
New anisocoria or ptosis suggesting an acquired neurological cause rather than a congenital condition
reference.prognosis: The ocular condition is stable and chiefly causes photophobia and near difficulty managed with optical measures, but prognosis in ACTA2-related cases is dominated by the potentially serious cardiovascular and cerebrovascular complications.
pitfalls: Assuming a neurological cause and pursuing unnecessary third nerve investigation
Overlooking the systemic ACTA2 associations and their vascular risks
Confusing it with pharmacological or traumatic mydriasis
references: Taylor & Hoyt's Paediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus
management: Optical management of photophobia and glare with tinted lenses, sunglasses and photochromic spectacles
Correction of refractive error and near difficulty with spectacles, including reading or bifocal correction
Tinted or artificial-pupil contact lenses to reduce the fixed large aperture for functional and cosmetic benefit
Genetic testing for ACTA2 and screening for the associated smooth-muscle dysfunction syndrome
Cardiovascular and cerebrovascular surveillance with echocardiography and aortic and cerebral vascular imaging in ACTA2-related disease, which dominates prognosis
Management of patent ductus arteriosus and aortic and cerebrovascular disease with the relevant specialists
Genetic counselling and family screening where an ACTA2 variant is confirmed
